etymology.text: 西 (‘west, Western’) + 红 (‘red’) + 柿 (‘persimmon’): the ‘red persimmon from the West’. Wiktionary marks the word as chiefly Mainland China, especially Mandarin.

funFacts: Both Chinese names say ‘foreign’: 西 ‘Western’ here and 番 ‘foreign’ in 番茄 — the tomato is an American plant that reached China only in late imperial times.
pitfalls: 柿 shì (persimmon) is 木 + 市 — don’t confuse it with 市 shì (market).
Ketchup is normally 番茄酱, even among people who call the tomato 西红柿.
subtleties: In the north 西红柿 is the everyday word; 番茄 dominates in the south, in Taiwan and in product names.

etymology.text: 菜 (‘vegetable’, especially a brassica) + 花 (‘flower’): the edible flower head.

funFacts: The Song poet Yang Wanli’s line 飞入菜花无处寻 (a butterfly lost among rapeseed blossoms) is a classroom favourite.
pitfalls: 菜花 can also mean rapeseed blossoms (油菜花) and, colloquially, genital warts — context makes it clear.
Broccoli is not 菜花 but 西兰花 (also 绿菜花 ‘green cauliflower’).
subtleties: Florets are counted with 朵 (like flowers): 一朵菜花.

etymology.text: 西 (‘West, Western’) + 兰 + 花 (‘flower’). Wiktionary marks the word as chiefly Mainland China, Hong Kong, Malaysia and Singapore; Taiwan says 青花菜.

funFacts: Broccoli, cauliflower and cabbage are all forms of one species, Brassica oleracea.
pitfalls: Also written 西蓝花 (蓝 ‘blue’); both spellings are in use.
Don’t read 兰花 here as ‘orchid’: 西兰花 is one word, broccoli.
subtleties: Florets are counted with 朵: 一朵西兰花.

etymology.text: 韭 (‘garlic chives’) + 葱 (‘scallion’): a compound of the names of two related plants.

funFacts: The leek is not a traditional Chinese vegetable — Chinese cooks reach for 大葱 or 韭菜 instead.
pitfalls: 韭菜 (garlic chives), 大葱 (Welsh onion) and 韭葱 (leek) are three different plants.
韭 jiǔ has the 3rd tone, like 九 jiǔ (nine).
subtleties: The leek is the national emblem of Wales; in that context the Chinese word is 韭葱.

etymology.text: 甜 (‘sweet’) + 椒 (‘pepper’, the family name of chilies and peppers).

funFacts: The shape-names 柿子椒 and 灯笼椒 compare the bell pepper to a persimmon and a lantern.
pitfalls: 青椒 is not always sweet; 甜椒 always is.
甜 tián (sweet) vs 田 tián (field): same sound, different meaning.
subtleties: Chinese names peppers by taste and shape: 甜椒 sweet, 辣椒 hot, 灯笼椒 ‘lantern’, 柿子椒 ‘persimmon’.

etymology.text: 甜菜 (‘sweet vegetable’ = beet) + 根 (‘root’).

funFacts: A large share of the world’s sugar is made from 甜菜 (sugar beet), the beetroot’s close relative.
pitfalls: 甜菜 alone often means the sugar beet; the table beet is 甜菜根 or 红菜头.
根 at the end is part of the word here, not the measure word.
subtleties: Borscht is 红菜汤 ‘red vegetable soup’, after the beetroot’s colour.

etymology.text: 四季 (‘the four seasons’) + 豆 (‘bean’): the ‘four-seasons bean’.

funFacts: 干煸 ‘dry-frying’ — frying the beans until their skins blister — is the signature Sichuan way to cook them.
pitfalls: Undercooked green beans can cause food poisoning — Chinese cooks always cook them through.
豆角 does not always mean the green bean: in many places it is the long yardlong bean (豇豆).
subtleties: Single beans are counted with 根; by weight: 一斤四季豆.

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 艸 (‘grass, plant’) + phonetic 悤. From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *b-tsoŋ (‘onion’); cognate with Tibetan བཙོང (btsong).

etymology.text: 芹 (‘celery’: semantic 艹 ‘plant’ + phonetic 斤) + 菜 (‘vegetable’).

funFacts: 献芹 ‘offering celery’ is an old humble way of presenting a modest gift or suggestion.
pitfalls: 芹 qín (2nd tone); 斤 jīn inside only hints at the sound.
Coriander is 香菜, not 芹菜.
subtleties: Chinese celery (芹菜) is thinner and stronger in taste than Western celery (西芹).

etymology.text: 玉 (‘jade’) + 米 (‘rice, hulled grain’): ‘jade grain’.
